examples.question_text: Mia wants to investigate students’ use of the school library. Her draft question is “Is the library popular?” Explain what needs clarification, then write a specific statistical question and a matching aim for Year $8$.
examples.solution_text:
“Popular” does not specify what each student should report.

Statistical question: How many times did each Year $8$ student visit the school library last week?

Aim: To find out how often Year $8$ students visited the school library last week.

The number of visits can vary between students.

examples.question_text:
An inquiry records how many times each Year $8$ student visited the library last week. Which hypothesis matches the inquiry? Explain your choice.

A. The library should buy more books.

B. More than half of Year $8$ students visited the library at least once last week.
examples.solution_text:
B predicts a result that the recorded visit counts can support or contradict.

A recommends an action; the visit counts alone cannot establish which books the library should buy.

examples.question_text:
A school wants to compare weekly reading time for Year $7$ and Year $10$ students. It surveys $32$ students from each year group, recording their year group and minutes spent reading last week.

State the population, sample and variables. Classify each variable.
examples.solution_text:
Population: all Year $7$ and Year $10$ students at the school.

Sample: the $64$ students surveyed.

Minutes spent reading last week is numerical: each student reports an amount.

Year group is categorical: it identifies the group each student belongs to.

examples.question_text:
Choose a suitable collection method for each inquiry and give a reason.

(a) Which lunchtime activity would students prefer?

(b) What are the lengths of leaves on the school’s shrubs?

(c) How many bicycles pass the school gate from $8$ am to $8{:}30$ am?

(d) How old are the trees in a park with dated planting records?
examples.solution_text:
(a) Survey students. Preferences must be reported by the students themselves.

(b) Measure the leaf lengths using the same unit and procedure for each leaf.

(c) Observe the gate and count bicycles during the specified period.

(d) Use the planting records to determine each tree’s age at a stated reference date.

examples.question_text:
A class plans to investigate students’ preferred lunchtime activities. Its survey requests names and home addresses, and the class intends to send individual responses to an advertising company.

Describe how the collection and use of the data should be changed.
examples.solution_text:
Explain the inquiry’s purpose before collecting responses and obtain consent; taking part should be voluntary.

Ask only for the preferred activity. Names and addresses are unnecessary for this aim.

Collect responses anonymously, store the data securely and report category totals.

Use the data only for the stated inquiry. Do not pass individual responses to the advertising company.

examples.question_text:
An inquiry records the preferred lunchtime activity of $15$ students:

reading, sport, music, sport, reading, sport, music, reading, sport, music, sport, reading, music, sport, reading.

Organise the responses into a frequency table and check the total.
examples.solution_text:
Tally each response once, then count each category.

| Activity | Frequency |
| --- | ---: |
| Reading | $5$ |
| Sport | $6$ |
| Music | $4$ |
| Total | $15$ |

The frequencies total $5+6+4=15$, matching the number of responses.

examples.question_text:
An inquiry records these journey times, in minutes, for $12$ students:

$6,\ 18,\ 11,\ 27,\ 9,\ 22,\ 14,\ 31,\ 19,\ 8,\ 25,\ 16$.

Organise the data into a frequency table using $0\leq t<10$, $10\leq t<20$, $20\leq t<30$ and $30\leq t<40$.
examples.solution_text:
Each interval includes its lower boundary and excludes its upper boundary.

| Journey time (minutes) | Frequency |
| --- | ---: |
| $0\leq t<10$ | $3$ |
| $10\leq t<20$ | $5$ |
| $20\leq t<30$ | $3$ |
| $30\leq t<40$ | $1$ |
| Total | $12$ |

The frequencies total $3+5+3+1=12$.

examples.question_text:
Choose a suitable display for each inquiry and explain why.

(a) Compare students’ preferred lunchtime activities.

(b) Compare the number of library visits made by Year $7$ and Year $10$ students.

(c) Investigate whether students with longer journeys travel greater distances.
examples.solution_text:
(a) A column graph compares the frequencies of the activity categories.

(b) Two dot plots on the same scale show the numerical visit counts for the two year groups.

(c) A scatter plot shows each student’s paired journey time and distance. Plot one point per student.

When planning a report, choose multiple displays that add useful information rather than repeating the same comparison.

Half of $24$ is $12$. The graph shows $14$ households prefer email, and $14>12$.

The sample data supports the hypothesis for the households surveyed.

All responses came from one apartment building. These households may not represent the wider community, so the report should not assume that more than half of all community households prefer email.

examples.question_text:
Put these stages of an inquiry into a sensible order.

A. Collect and organise the responses ethically.

B. Identify the population and variables.

C. Display the data and report the findings.

D. State the aim and hypothesis.

E. Choose the collection method and sample.
examples.solution_text:
D, B, E, A, C.

The aim and hypothesis determine which population and variables are needed. Choose the collection method and sample before gathering data. Organise the collected responses before displaying and reporting the findings.

examples.question_text:
A school wants to investigate whether Year $10$ students visit the library more often than Year $7$ students.

A student proposes:

Hypothesis: Reading is important.

Collection: Ask $18$ friends in Year $10$, “Do you enjoy reading?”

Display: A scatter plot.

Identify and correct the hypothesis, collection and display problems. Include an ethical safeguard.
examples.solution_text:
Hypothesis: “Year $10$ students visit the library more often in a school week than Year $7$ students.” This predicts a difference the data can investigate.

Collection: Record the number of library visits in the same school week and the year group for each participant. Randomly select students from each of the full Year $7$ and Year $10$ lists. Asking only Year $10$ friends excludes the comparison group and may give an unrepresentative sample; enjoyment of reading does not measure library visits.

Display: Use two dot plots on the same scale. Visit count is numerical and year group is categorical; this is not a pair of numerical variables for a scatter plot.

Ethical safeguard: explain the purpose, obtain voluntary consent and collect responses without names.

examples.derivation: Visit counts specify a variable, population and reference period, with variation expected between students. The aim matches that question.
B can be tested by counting students with at least one visit and comparing with half the year group. A recommends an action rather than predicting visit counts.
The population contains both complete year groups; the sample contains 32+32=64 students. Reading minutes are numerical and year group is categorical.
Preferences require a survey, leaf lengths require measurement, passing bicycles require observation, and dated planting records provide tree ages relative to a stated date.
Voluntary informed participation, collecting only necessary anonymous responses, secure storage and reporting totals address the collection and disclosure problems.
Reading occurs at positions 1,5,8,12,15; sport at 2,4,6,9,11,14; music at 3,7,10,13. Frequencies are 5,6,4 and total 15.
The intervals contain {6,9,8}, {18,11,14,19,16}, {27,22,25} and {31}, respectively. Frequencies are 3,5,3,1 and total 12.
Activity categories suit a column graph; numerical visit counts across two categorical year groups suit comparable dot plots; paired numerical journey times and distances suit a scatter plot.

The diagram encodes email 14, print 6 and app 4, totalling 24. Half is 12 and 14>12. One-building sampling limits conclusions about the wider community. The planar diagram uses black unshaded outlines, consistent labels and explicit typography.
D establishes the aim and hypothesis; B identifies required population and variables; E plans collection; A gathers and organises responses; C displays and reports them.

A comparative library-visit hypothesis matches the aim. Recording visit counts over the same week from randomly selected members of both year groups repairs the variable and sampling mismatches. Comparable dot plots suit numerical counts grouped by year; voluntary consent and anonymous responses provide ethical safeguards.
